kurals.tamil:
இறந்த வெகுளியின் தீதே சிறந்த
உவகை மகிழ்ச்சியிற் சோர்வு.
kurals.transliteration:
Irandha vekuliyin theedhe sirandha
Uvakai makizhchchiyir sorvu.
kurals.meaning: Getting careless because you are carried away by great joy does more harm than even anger that has gone past all limits.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a team that is winning a game by a lot. The players start celebrating early, stop paying attention, and the other team sneaks back and wins. Getting too excited and careless can hurt you even more than losing your temper, because you don't even notice the danger coming.
kurals.university: The chapter title பொச்சாவாமை is the negative verbal noun of பொச்சா- (‘to forget, to be negligent’; compare பொச்சாப்பு, ‘forgetfulness, heedlessness’). So it names a positive discipline of not forgetting, and because it sits in the Arasiyal (royal conduct) section, Parimelazhagar reads the whole chapter as advice to a king. In this couplet சோர்வு is the lapse or slackening born of சிறந்த உவகை மகிழ்ச்சி, ‘the delight of surpassing joy’, and இறந்த வெகுளி is anger that has gone past all bounds. Parimelazhagar says that such joy comes from great wealth, great pleasure and great pride. He explains the comparison this way: measured anger is needed to crush enemies and punish the wicked, and even excessive anger may sometimes kill a foe, but forgetfulness born of joy kills only the person who has it, so it is the worse evil. Manakkudavar agrees on the sense but records another way to read the phrase, as the joy one directs towards those one must favour. Pavanar follows Parimelazhagar. The emphatic ஏ in தீதே underlines the surprising verdict that the pleasant fault is worse than the violent one.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He whom neither anger nor joy, nor pride, nor false modesty, nor stupefaction, nor vanity, can draw away from the high ends of life, is considered as wise.”
hinduism.explanation: The anxious king Dhritarashtra cannot sleep, and Vidura counsels him through the night. Vidura says a wise man is someone who is pulled away from his true aims neither by the heat of anger nor by the glow of joy.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural pairs the same two forces, anger and joy, and warns that joy is the more treacherous distraction.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: Vidura names anger and joy together as forces that pull a person from his aims, but he doesn't rank joy as the worse of the two.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life, and so that day come upon you unawares.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that indulgence and worldly absorption dull the heart, so that the decisive moment arrives while one is unprepared.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats being overfull with pleasure as the thing that makes a person careless.
christianity._accuracy_note: Clear match on indulgence leading to unreadiness; the comparison with anger is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing the enemy by His permission until [the time] when you lost courage and fell to disputing about the order [given by the Prophet] and disobeyed after He had shown you that which you love.”
islam.explanation: At Uhud the Muslim archers had been told never to leave their hill. When victory and its spoils seemed certain they left their post, and the enemy cavalry turned the battle against them.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's danger exactly: slackness born of the joy of apparent success, which turns victory into defeat.
islam.source: Qur'an 3:152 (Saheeh International), with the Uhud narrative in the sira literature
islam._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match. The verse also stresses disobedience and dispute, not only forgetful elation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “lest when thou hast eaten and art satisfied, and hast built goodly houses, and dwelt therein; and when thy herds and thy flocks multiply, and thy silver and thy gold is multiplied, and all that thou hast is multiplied; then thy heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God”
judaism.explanation: Moses warns Israel that prosperity in the promised land will be the moment of greatest danger, because abundance swells the heart and breeds forgetting.
judaism.tie_back: The Torah and the Kural both name forgetfulness born of prosperity and joy as the special peril of the successful.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-exact thematic match: prosperity leading to a lifted-up heart and forgetfulness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do not give way to heedlessness. Do not indulge in sensual pleasures. Only the heedful and meditative attain great happiness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha links heedlessness (pamāda) directly to indulgence in pleasure and sets heedfulness against both.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural too finds the root of carelessness in pleasure and delight.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Same link between pleasure and heedlessness; no comparison with anger.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Theseus kills the Minotaur and sails home from Crete. He and his pilot are so overjoyed at their success that they forget to raise the white sail that was meant to signal his safety. His father Aegeus sees the black sail from the cliffs, believes his son is dead, and throws himself to his death.
greek_mythology.explanation: The triumph was complete, but a single lapse caused by the joy of victory turned it into tragedy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's forgetfulness born of great joy, and its cost was worse than any enemy's anger.
greek_mythology.source: Plutarch, Life of Theseus 22; also Catullus 64
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Plutarch explicitly attributes the forgotten sail to joy at their success; an almost literal illustration.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “the offences which are committed through desire are more blameable than those which are committed through anger”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius approves Theophrastus's view that a fault committed under pleasure is worse than one committed in anger, because anger at least turns from reason with pain, while pleasure carries a person along willingly.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the same counter-intuitive ranking, placing the pleasant failing above the violent one.
philosophy.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 2.10 (trans. George Long), reporting Theophrastus
philosophy._accuracy_note: The same ranking of pleasure-driven failure above anger, though Marcus is talking about blame for offences, not about forgetfulness.

kurals.tamil:
பொச்சாப்புக் கொல்லும் புகழை அறிவினை
நிச்ச நிரப்புக்கொன் றாங்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Pochchaappuk kollum pukazhai arivinai
Nichcha nirappuk kon raangu.
kurals.meaning: Just as grinding, day-after-day poverty kills a person's intelligence, forgetfulness kills a person's good name.
kurals.elementary: If a child is hungry every single day, it is very hard for them to think clearly at school. In the same way, if someone keeps forgetting their promises and jobs, people slowly stop trusting and admiring them, until their good name is gone.
kurals.university: The verb கொல்லும் (‘kills’) does strong work in both halves: பொச்சாப்பு kills புகழ் (fame) just as நிச்ச நிரப்பு kills அறிவு (understanding). Parimelazhagar glosses நிச்ச நிரப்பு as filling one's belly every day by begging. When this happens to a learned man, the humiliation and sin involved bring contempt on him and destroy the regard he enjoyed. In the same way, forgetfulness in a man of fame brings contempt, because he fails to guard himself and his affairs fall apart, and so it destroys his standing. Pavanar notes that நிரப்பு (literally ‘fullness’) is an auspicious euphemism for poverty, and he cross-refers to Kural 1046, where even the sound words of the poor go unheeded. Manakkudavar reads this couplet as part of a set on holding firm in worldly affairs. Parimelazhagar groups 531-532 as the couplets that state the fault of heedlessness. Editions split the final words either as நிரப்புக்கொன் றாங்கு or as நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு; the sense is the same.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Anger leads to clouding of judgment, which results in bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, the intellect gets destroyed; and when the intellect is destroyed, one is ruined.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces the downward chain in which the loss of smṛti (memory, mindfulness) destroys discernment and finally the person.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita treats a failure of remembering as something that kills, not merely inconveniences.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Both trace a path from lost memory to ruin, but the Gita starts from anger and speaks of inner ruin, not lost reputation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I know thy works, that thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead. Be watchful, and strengthen the things which remain, that are ready to die”
christianity.explanation: The church at Sardis still has a reputation for life, but through lack of watchfulness it has become spiritually dead, and it is told to wake up before what remains dies too.
christianity.tie_back: This is a good name emptied out by heedlessness, which is exactly the loss the Kural describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: A striking parallel of reputation (‘a name’) and death through lack of watchfulness.

islam.quote_or_event: “And be not like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves. Those are the defiantly disobedient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an presents forgetting God as self-destroying: the forgetful end up losing even their own selves and their true standing.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, forgetfulness is not a small slip but something that eats away what a person is worth.
islam._accuracy_note: Forgetfulness as self-destruction fits well; the Qur'an's object is God rather than worldly duties or fame.

judaism.quote_or_event: “whoever forgets one word of his study, scripture accounts it to him as if he were mortally guilty”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Meir, basing himself on Deuteronomy 4:9, treats the careless forgetting of what one has learned as a matter of life and death, though he excuses forgetting that happens despite real effort.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats forgetfulness as something that can kill.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:8, trans. Joshua Kulp
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that forgetting is deadly; it concerns Torah learning rather than public reputation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ever grows the glory of him who is energetic, mindful and pure in conduct, discerning and self-controlled, righteous and heedful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada ties a person's glory (yasa) directly to heedfulness and mindfulness.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the positive side of the Kural: heedfulness makes glory grow, and heedlessness kills it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Directly links fame or glory with heedfulness, stated from the positive side.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Elpenor, the youngest of Odysseus's crew, is heavy with wine and falls asleep on Circe's roof. Woken by the noise of departure, he forgets to use the ladder, falls, and breaks his neck. In the underworld he begs Odysseus for a burial mound so that men to come will know of him.
greek_mythology.explanation: One moment of forgetfulness costs Elpenor his life and nearly his memory among men, which he has to plead for.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's point is that heedlessness kills a person's name, and Elpenor's fate shows it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A clear case of a careless lapse destroying a man and threatening his remembrance, but it is a personal accident, not a decline of reputation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca opens his letters to Lucilius by observing that some of our time is snatched away and some slips from us, but that the most disgraceful loss of all is the one caused by our own carelessness.
philosophy.explanation: For Seneca the losses we cause through negligence are worse than those forced on us, because they were within our power to prevent.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise says heedlessness steadily wastes something precious, in this case a good name.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 1 (trans. R. M. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased. Same idea of self-inflicted loss through carelessness, but it is about time, not fame.

kurals.tamil:
பொச்சாப்பார்க் கில்லை புகழ்மை அதுஉலகத்து
எப்பால்நூ லோர்க்கும் துணிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Pochchaappaark killai pukazhmai adhuulakaththu
Eppaalnoo lorkkum thunivu.
kurals.meaning: The forgetful never win lasting fame. On this point, the authors of every kind of treatise in the world agree.
kurals.elementary: Ask a coach, a music teacher, a doctor, or a chef, and they will all tell you the same thing: people who keep forgetting and not paying attention never become great at anything. When everyone agrees on something, it's worth listening!
kurals.university: புகழ்மை means ‘the state of having fame’, and துணிவு here means a settled conclusion, not courage. Parimelazhagar takes எப்பால் நூலோர் to mean the authors of treatises of every kind, not only of polity (நீதி நூல்). He explains that the rule holds for everyone, not only kings: anyone pursuing any of the four aims of life (aṟam, poruḷ, iṉpam, vīṭu) will fail if heedless, and so will have no fame. Pavanar agrees that the rule is universal but argues that உலகம் here means the Tamil world and that எப்பால் நூல் refers to the branches of Tamil learning, much of which has since been lost; he points out that Valluvar does not say the northern (Sanskrit) texts agree. Manakkudavar reads the couplet simply as saying that heedlessness brings no fame. Parimelazhagar groups 533-535 as describing the harm (ஏதம்) that comes to the heedless.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The six faults should be avoided by a person who wisheth to attain prosperity, viz., sleep, drowsiness, fear, anger, indolence and procrastination.”
hinduism.explanation: Vidura's statecraft maxims, in the nīti tradition, list the forms of inattention (sleep, drowsiness, idleness, delay) among the faults that rule out prosperity.
hinduism.tie_back: This confirms the Kural's claim that the treatise writers agree: the nīti texts too hold that the heedless cannot prosper.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Section 33 (Vidura Niti), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: A nīti authority naming faults of heedlessness as barriers to success; it does not speak of fame or make the Kural's appeal to consensus.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping. And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus ends his discourse on the last things by extending the command to watch beyond his disciples to everyone.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it presents watchfulness as a rule that holds universally, not a counsel for a few.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the universal scope and the demand for vigilance; it says nothing about fame.

islam.quote_or_event: “They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray. It is they who are the heedless.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an names the heedless (al-ghāfilūn) as the lowest of the low: people who have every faculty and use none.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it places heedlessness (ghaflah) beneath all honour.
islam._accuracy_note: A strong condemnation of heedlessness; the Kural's specific point about fame and scholarly consensus is not present.

judaism.quote_or_event: In Mesillat Yesharim, Moshe Chaim Luzzatto builds his ladder of spiritual ascent on the baraita of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair (Avodah Zarah 20b), which starts from watchfulness (zehirut). He makes watchfulness the first rung and argues that a person who goes through life without examining his ways is like someone walking blind along a riverbank.
judaism.explanation: Luzzatto draws together a classic rabbinic chain of virtues in which careful watchfulness is the foundation for every higher attainment.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural's ‘all treatises agree’, the Jewish ethical tradition treats vigilance as the agreed starting point without which nothing worthy is achieved.
judaism.source: Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, Mesillat Yesharim, chs. 1-2 (on Zehirut); Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 20b
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased summary. Watchfulness is foundational in both, but Luzzatto's goal is holiness, not fame.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “By Heedfulness did Indra become the overlord of the gods. Heedfulness is ever praised, and heedlessness ever despised.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada states a universal verdict: heedfulness is always praised and heedlessness always despised, and it cites even Indra's rise as proof.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's ‘settled conclusion of all’: the heedless get no praise.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: a general verdict that heedlessness is never praised.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Some of Odysseus's men eat the honey-sweet lotus and forget all thought of home. They want only to stay among the Lotus-eaters, and Odysseus has to drag them weeping back to the ships and tie them down.
greek_mythology.explanation: The lotus stands for any pleasure that wipes out memory of one's purpose. The men who ate it would have lost their homecoming (nostos), and with it any share in the hero's glory.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural says the forgetful win no fame, and those who forget their homecoming vanish from the story.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A classic image of pleasure-induced forgetfulness; the link to fame has to be inferred.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pierre Hadot argued that prosoche, continuous attention to oneself and to the present moment, was the fundamental spiritual attitude of the Stoics, and that practices of vigilance were shared across the ancient schools of philosophy.
philosophy.explanation: Hadot's reading of ancient philosophy as a set of ‘spiritual exercises’ puts attention at the core of the Stoic and wider philosophical way of life.
philosophy.tie_back: Hadot's account supports the Kural's claim that the ‘authors of every kind of treatise’ agree on the value of unforgetting vigilance.
philosophy.source: Pierre Hadot, Philosophy as a Way of Life, ed. Arnold I. Davidson (Blackwell, 1995), essay ‘Spiritual Exercises’
philosophy._accuracy_note: A secondary-source summary. Good support for the broad consensus on attention, but it doesn't discuss fame.

kurals.tamil:
அச்ச முடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை ஆங்கில்லை
பொச்சாப் புடையார்க்கு நன்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Achcha mutaiyaarkku aranillai aangillai
Pochchaap putaiyaarkku nanku.
kurals.meaning: No fortress helps someone who is afraid at heart, and in the same way no advantage helps someone who is heedless.
kurals.elementary: A castle with tall walls won't help a guard who is too scared to stand at his post. And a house full of good locks won't help if you forget to lock the door. What really protects you is what's going on inside your own head.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a simile (உவமை) marked by ஆங்கு (‘in the same way’). Fear inside makes outer defences (அரண்) useless, and forgetfulness inside makes outer goods (நன்கு) useless. Parimelazhagar spells out the அரண் as forest, mountain and similar strongholds, and glosses நன்கு as wealth of every kind, called ‘the good’ because it is a means to good. His conclusion is that just as the stronghold of the fearful falls, the riches of the heedless perish. Pavanar adds armies to the list of advantages and derives நன்கு from நல் > நன். Manakkudavar sums the couplet up as saying that the heedless have no protection. By pairing அச்சம் (fear) with பொச்சாப்பு (heedlessness), Valluvar treats both as inner failures of a ruler's mind that no outward resource can make up for.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One must deliver himself with the help of his mind, and not degrade himself. The mind is the friend of the conditioned soul, and his enemy as well.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that the decisive ally or enemy is one's own mind, not any outer circumstance.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural too says an inner defect, fear or forgetfulness, cancels every outward protection.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.5 (Bhagavad-gita As It Is, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Both put the inner state before outer circumstance, but the Gita doesn't mention fortresses or heedlessness directly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But know this, that if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched, and would not have suffered his house to be broken up.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points out that a house is lost not for lack of walls but for lack of watching.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's point: defences and possessions are useless to someone who is not vigilant.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on a protected house lost through failure to watch.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah has already given you victory in many regions and [even] on the day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you, but it did not avail you at all, and the earth was confining for you with its vastness; then you turned back, fleeing.”
islam.explanation: At Hunayn the Muslim army trusted in its unprecedented size and was ambushed and scattered at first.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, a great outward advantage is worth nothing when the mind is complacent.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on outward strength failing because of an inner state of complacency.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then the five men departed, and came to Laish, and saw the people that were therein, how they dwelt in security, after the manner of the Zidonians, quiet and secure; for there was none in the land, possessing authority, that might put them to shame in any thing, and they were far from the Zidonians, and had no dealings with any man.”
judaism.explanation: The Danite spies find Laish rich, remote and carelessly at ease. The tribe soon comes against the unsuspecting city and burns it (Judges 18:27-28).
judaism.tie_back: Laish had every natural advantage but no vigilance, and its good fortune did it no good, as the Kural says.
judaism._accuracy_note: A good narrative match: a prosperous, secure city destroyed through complacency.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “By effort and heedfulness, discipline and self-mastery, let the wise one make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.”
buddhism.explanation: The only true refuge, the Buddha says, is an island built within oneself out of effort and heedfulness.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural too places real security in the inner state, not in outer walls.
buddhism._accuracy_note: An inner island of heedfulness set against outer defences; a close conceptual fit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Aeolus gives Odysseus all the adverse winds tied up in an ox-hide bag, and the west wind carries his fleet home. With Ithaca in sight, Odysseus, worn out from steering for nine days, falls asleep. His crew open the bag hoping to find treasure, and the storm blows them all the way back.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus had every advantage a sailor could want, and lost it all in one lapse of watchfulness.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's heedless man, for whom even the greatest good fortune does no good.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: An excellent illustration of advantages made useless by a lapse in vigilance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli asks whether fortresses are useful to princes. He concludes that they help or harm according to circumstances, that the best fortress is not to be hated by one's people, and that the Countess of Forlì's citadel did not save her in the end.
philosophy.explanation: For Machiavelli the stone walls matter less than the political condition inside them.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's thought is similar: a stronghold cannot make up for a defect within.
philosophy.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 20 (trans. W. K. Marriott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased. Shares the insight that fortresses are useless without the right inner condition, though for Machiavelli that condition is popular goodwill, not vigilance.

kurals.tamil:
முன்னுறக் காவாது இழுக்கியான் தன்பிழை
பின்னூறு இரங்கி விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Munnurak kaavaadhu izhukkiyaan thanpizhai
Pinnooru irangi vitum.
kurals.meaning: Someone who carelessly fails to guard against trouble before it comes will be left grieving over his own mistake once it strikes.
kurals.elementary: If you know a test is coming and you don't study, you'll feel terrible when you see questions you can't answer. Getting ready before trouble comes is much better than feeling sorry afterwards.
kurals.university: முன் உற (‘before it arrives’) and பின் ஊறு (‘when the blow has fallen’) frame the couplet in time, and இழுக்கியான் (‘one who slipped, was negligent’) is described by காவாது (‘without guarding’). Parimelazhagar says the troubles in view are those that can be guarded against, namely what enemies do when they spot a lapse. He treats ஊறு as standing for ஊற்றின்கண், with both the case-ending and the linking syllable dropped, and explains இரங்கிவிடும் as ‘will be left to grieve’, because once the trouble has come it can no longer be warded off. Pavanar widens the preventable troubles to include famine and flood, and takes விடும் in the sense of ‘perishing’. Manakkudavar's gloss is almost word for word the same as Parimelazhagar's. This couplet closes Parimelazhagar's group of three (533-535) on the harm that comes to the heedless.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra three fish live in a pond: Anāgatavidhātā (‘Forethought’), Pratyutpannamati (‘Ready-wit’) and Yadbhaviṣya (‘Whatever-will-be’). When fishermen are overheard planning to net the pond, Forethought leaves at once and Ready-wit escapes by playing dead, but Whatever-will-be does nothing and is caught.
hinduism.explanation: This nīti fable, told to princes, contrasts the one who guards in advance with the one who waits and is lost.
hinduism.tie_back: Yadbhaviṣya is exactly the Kural's heedless man, whose failure to act beforehand leaves no remedy afterwards.
hinduism.source: Panchatantra, Book I (Mitrabheda), the fable of the three fish
hinduism._accuracy_note: A near-perfect narrative parallel to guarding before trouble arrives; retold in prose.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut. Afterward came also the other virgins, saying, Lord, Lord, open to us. But he answered and said, Verily I say unto you, I know you not. Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh.”
christianity.explanation: The foolish virgins brought no spare oil. By the time they had gone to fetch it, the door was shut, and their pleading came too late.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's picture of someone who did not provide beforehand and can only lament afterwards.
christianity._accuracy_note: A very close match on failing to prepare and regretting too late.

islam.quote_or_event: “And spend [in the way of Allah] from what We have provided you before death approaches one of you and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I would give charity and be among the righteous."”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an pictures the person who put off good deeds, begging too late for a little more time.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's pattern: neglect beforehand, then useless lament once the moment has passed.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on regret that comes too late after negligence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “one should repent today lest he die tomorrow; and by following this advice one will spend his entire life in a state of repentance.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer's advice is to ‘repent one day before your death’. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai adds a parable of a king who invites his servants to a feast without fixing the hour: the wise dress and wait at the door, while the foolish go off to work and are caught unprepared when the call comes.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Talmud teaches that you should be ready before the day of reckoning, because afterwards there is only regret.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match on readiness before an unannounced crisis; the parable adds the image of the unprepared fools.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a border city is closely guarded both within and without, even so, guard yourself. Do not let slip this opportunity (for spiritual growth). For those who let slip this opportunity grieve indeed when consigned to hell.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the self to a frontier town that has to be guarded before attack, and warns that those who let the moment slip will grieve afterwards.
buddhism.tie_back: It has the same structure as the Kural: guard in advance, or grieve when the harm arrives.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close, including the guarded city and the later grief of those who were negligent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus (‘Forethought’) warned his brother Epimetheus (‘Afterthought’) never to accept a gift from Zeus. Epimetheus forgot the warning and took Pandora, and he understood the evil only once it was already his.
greek_mythology.explanation: The two brothers' names are themselves a lesson: one sees ahead, the other only understands after the damage is done.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Epimetheus is the Kural's man who did not guard beforehand and could only realize his error afterwards.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: An almost allegorical match: forgetting a warning, then understanding too late.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Explaining why the Italian princes lost their states, Machiavelli says that in quiet times they never thought things could change, which he calls a common human fault of not reckoning on the storm during fair weather. When adversity came, they thought of flight instead of defence.
philosophy.explanation: For Machiavelli, rulers fall less through bad luck than through failing to prepare while they still could.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's heedless ruler, who did not guard in advance and is left lamenting.
philosophy.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, ch. 24 (trans. W. K. Marriott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased. A strong political parallel on failure to prepare in calm times.

kurals.tamil:
இழுக்காமை யார்மாட்டும் என்றும் வழுக்காமை
வாயின் அதுவொப்பது இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Izhukkaamai yaarmaattum endrum vazhukkaamai
Vaayin adhuvoppadhu il.
kurals.meaning: If a person can keep up unfailing watchfulness towards everyone and at all times, no other good can equal it.
kurals.elementary: Being careful once is easy. Being careful with everyone, every day, even when things are going great, is the real superpower. If you can do that, it's better than almost any other gift you could have.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on two near-synonyms: இழுக்காமை (‘not slipping’, that is, unforgetfulness) must be present வழுக்காமை (‘without a lapse’). Parimelazhagar explains யார்மாட்டும் as reaching even the king's own people, the servants who do his work and his kin, and என்றும் as meaning ‘in days of growth and of decline alike’. He parses வாயின் as a conditional form built on the verbal-noun stem வாய் (‘to come right, to fall into place’). Pavanar adds that வழுக்காமை means applying this without fail in every task, and he explicitly rejects Parimelazhagar's analysis of வாயின், citing Tolkāppiyam and Kural 737 to argue that வாய் is an intransitive verb. Manakkudavar reads the couplet as a rule for the careful administration of justice. Together with 537, this couplet forms Parimelazhagar's pair on the excellence of unforgetfulness.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Therefore, Arjuna, you should always think of Me in the form of Kṛṣṇa and at the same time carry out your prescribed duty of fighting. With your activities dedicated to Me and your mind and intelligence fixed on Me, you will attain Me without doubt.”
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit sarveṣu kāleṣu anusmara means ‘remember at all times’. Krishna asks for unbroken remembrance to go along with, not replace, active duty.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's ideal is likewise remembrance that never lapses, ‘at all times’, while one carries on one's work.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 8.7 (Bhagavad-gita As It Is, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Both ask for remembrance at all times; the Gita's object is devotional, the Kural's practical.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:”
christianity.explanation: Peter calls for constant sobriety and alertness because the danger is always prowling nearby.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats unbroken vigilance as the essential safeguard.
christianity._accuracy_note: A direct call to continual vigilance; it doesn't state that nothing else is equal to it.

islam.quote_or_event: “And remember your Lord within yourself in humility and in fear without being apparent in speech - in the mornings and the evenings. And do not be among the heedless.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an asks for remembrance (dhikr) morning and evening, as a standing guard against ghaflah, heedlessness.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats unbroken remembrance as the positive virtue that defeats heedlessness.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on constant remembrance as the opposite of heedlessness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget the things which thine eyes saw, and lest they depart from thy heart all the days of thy life;”
judaism.explanation: Moses commands a watchfulness that lasts ‘all the days of thy life’ so that what has been learned is never forgotten.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's unforgetfulness kept up at all times.
judaism._accuracy_note: A very close match: lifelong, diligent guarding against forgetfulness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as the footprints of all living beings with legs can be encompassed by the footprint of the elephant, and the elephant's footprint is declared to be supreme among them in terms of its great size; in the same way, heedfulness is the one quality that keeps both kinds of benefit secure — benefits in this life & benefits in lives to come.”
buddhism.explanation: King Pasenadi asks the Buddha whether one quality secures every kind of welfare, and the Buddha names heedfulness (appamāda) as supreme among them all.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ‘nothing equals it’, stated almost word for word in Buddhist terms.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 3.17 (Appamada Sutta), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: An exceptionally close match: heedfulness declared to be the unequalled good, and addressed to a king.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hera sets Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed watchman, to guard Io. Only some of his eyes ever sleep at a time while the rest keep watch, until Hermes lulls every eye shut with his pipes and a long story and kills him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Argus is the Greek image of constant vigilance. His death shows that one lapse undoes everything.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural values watchfulness that never lapses at any time, and Argus's end shows why ‘always’ matters.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A cautionary illustration of constant vigilance and its one fatal lapse, not a statement of its supreme value.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In his discourse on attention (prosoche), Epictetus warns that once you relax your attention you should not imagine you can recover it whenever you like. Each lapse makes the next one easier and builds a habit of neglect, so attention has to be kept up continuously.
philosophy.explanation: For Epictetus vigilance is not a single act but an unbroken state, and any intermission costs more than it seems to.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's ideal of never slipping, towards anyone, at any time, matches Epictetus's demand exactly.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased. A strong conceptual match on continuous, unfailing attention.

kurals.tamil:
அரியஎன்று ஆகாத இல்லைபொச் சாவாக்
கருவியால் போற்றிச் செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ariyaendru aakaadha illaipoch chaavaak
Karuviyaal potrich cheyin.
kurals.meaning: No task is too hard to accomplish, however difficult it is said to be, if a person does it carefully, using an unforgetting mind as the tool.
kurals.elementary: Building a huge Lego castle sounds impossible. But if you keep the picture in your head, follow each step carefully, and don't lose track, you can finish it. A mind that doesn't forget is like a super-tool that makes hard jobs possible.
kurals.university: அரிய என்று ஆகாத இல்லை is a double negative: ‘there is nothing that, being called difficult, cannot be done’. Parimelazhagar takes பொச்சாவாக் கருவி to mean ‘the unforgetting mind’. On his reading, பொச்சாவாத has lost its final syllable by poetic licence, and the mind is called கருவி (‘instrument’) because it is the inner instrument (அந்தக்கரணம்); போற்றிச் செயின் means ‘if one does it with careful thought’. His summary is that people with unbroken attention and sound planning accomplish everything easily. Pavanar calls this gloss over-learned and prefers to read பொச்சாவாக் கருவி as an appositional compound, ‘the instrument that is unforgetfulness’. Manakkudavar likewise glosses it as மறவாமையாகிய கருவி. Modern commentators such as Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah reflect both readings.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O mighty-armed son of Kuntī, it is undoubtedly very difficult to curb the restless mind, but it is possible by suitable practice and by detachment.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna protests that the mind is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna grants that it is hard but insists that disciplined practice (abhyāsa) makes it possible.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita says that what is called ‘too hard’ becomes achievable through a steadily disciplined mind.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.35 (Bhagavad-gita As It Is, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Both move from ‘difficult’ to ‘possible’ through a disciplined mind; the Gita's object is mastering the mind itself.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
christianity.explanation: In Gethsemane Jesus gives watchfulness joined to prayer as the means by which a weak human nature can hold firm.
christianity.tie_back: Vigilance here is the tool that overcomes weakness, as the Kural's ‘instrument of unforgetfulness’ overcomes difficulty.
christianity._accuracy_note: Watchfulness is presented as the remedy for weakness, but the verse is less confident than the Kural about what vigilance can achieve.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who strive for Us - We will surely guide them to Our ways. And indeed, Allah is with the doers of good.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an promises that sustained striving (jihād in its broad sense) will be met with guidance to the way through.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that persistent, careful effort opens paths that seemed closed.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches on persistent effort overcoming obstacles; the specific instrument of unforgetfulness is not named.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud records Rabbi Yitzḥak's maxim: if someone tells you they laboured and did not find, do not believe them; if they say they found without labouring, do not believe them; but if they say they laboured and found, believe them.
judaism.explanation: The teaching insists that real attainment, especially in Torah, comes only through sustained, careful effort, and that such effort does not fail.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too holds that diligent, attentive work makes even the ‘impossible’ achievable.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of a well-known passage. Same confidence that diligent effort succeeds, without the Kural's emphasis on memory.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The monk who delights in heedfulness and looks with fear at heedlessness advances like fire, burning all fetters, small and large.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pictures heedfulness as a fire that consumes every obstacle, large or small.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's unforgetting instrument, heedfulness here overcomes every difficulty in its way.
buddhism._accuracy_note: A close match on heedfulness overcoming all obstacles, great and small.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Warned by Circe, Odysseus plugs his crew's ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast, ordering that his bonds be tightened if he begs to be freed. In this way he alone hears the Sirens' song and survives it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus knows his own mind will lapse under the song's spell, so he builds a device that keeps his resolve in force when his memory of it fails.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The mast and ropes are literally an ‘instrument of unforgetfulness’, and with them he achieves what no one had survived before.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: An apt image of a tool that secures vigilance against lapse; the idea of an ‘impossible’ task is implied, not stated.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Every moment think steadily as a Roman and a man to do what thou hast in hand with perfect and simple dignity, and feeling of affection, and freedom, and justice; and to give thyself relief from all other thoughts.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus urges full, steady attention to whatever task is in hand, putting away carelessness and distraction.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's ‘doing with care through an unforgetting mind’, turned into a daily discipline.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the attentive, careful doing; the promise that nothing is impossible is not stated.

kurals.tamil:
புகழ்ந்தவை போற்றிச் செயல்வேண்டும் செய்யாது
இகழ்ந்தார்க்கு எழுமையும் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pukazhndhavai potrich cheyalventum seyyaadhu
Ikazhndhaarkku ezhumaiyum il.
kurals.meaning: One must carefully do the things the wise have praised. For those who neglect them and leave them undone, there is no good in any of their seven births.
kurals.elementary: Your teachers and parents tell you some things are really worth doing, like being kind, doing homework, and telling the truth. Knowing that isn't enough; you have to actually do them. People who shrug those things off miss out on good things again and again.
kurals.university: புகழ்ந்தவை means ‘the things praised’. Parimelazhagar identifies them as the duties that works on polity single out as proper to kings: the three powers, the four expedients (upāya), the five kinds of action, the six policies, and so on. இகழ்ந்தார் here does not mean ‘those who scorned’; all the commentators take it as ‘those who neglected or forgot’, and Parimelazhagar glosses it as மறந்தவர். He reads எழுமையும் இல் as ‘no good in all seven births’, on the ground that those who fall away from their proper duty reap only suffering in hell, and he treats எழுமை (‘sevenfoldness’) as a metonymy. Pavanar rejects Parimelazhagar's appeal to caste duty (சாதி தருமம்) as foreign to the text, lists instead celebrated deeds of the ancient Tamil kings as examples of ‘praised acts’, and reads எழுமை as a conventional number. Parimelazhagar says this couplet sets out what must be done without forgetting.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Perform your prescribed duty, for doing so is better than not working. One cannot even maintain one’s physical body without work.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna urges Arjuna to carry out his prescribed duty (niyataṃ karma) instead of neglecting it.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural too insists that recommended duties be actually performed and warns of what follows from neglecting them.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.8 (Bhagavad-gita As It Is, A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the call to do one's prescribed duties; the Kural's stress on forgetting them and the seven births are not present.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass: For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was.”
christianity.explanation: James says that hearing what is good without doing it is a kind of forgetting, like glancing in a mirror and walking away.
christianity.tie_back: This matches the Kural closely: the praised deeds must be done, and failing to do them is described as forgetting.
christianity._accuracy_note: An exceptionally close match, even treating neglect of known duty as forgetfulness.

islam.quote_or_event: “There are two blessings that many people are deceived into losing: health and free time.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet warns that many people squander health and leisure, the very means for doing good, and lose them without noticing.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too warns that neglecting to do the praised deeds, while one still can, leaves a person with nothing.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches on the loss that comes from neglecting good opportunities; it doesn't name specific praised deeds.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Study is not the most important thing, but actions; whoever indulges in too many words brings about sin.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon ben Gamliel teaches that the point of learning is doing: knowledge of the good means nothing unless it is carried out.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural says the same: what the wise praise must be done, not merely admired.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 1:17, trans. Joshua Kulp
judaism._accuracy_note: Clear agreement that deeds, not knowledge, are primary.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like a beautiful flower full of color but without fragrance, even so, fruitless are the fair words of one who does not practice them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that praising the good without practising it is like a showy flower with no scent.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it insists that praised deeds bear fruit only when they are actually done.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the gap between praising and doing; it lacks the Kural's warning about consequences in later births.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Oeneus of Calydon offers harvest first-fruits to all the gods but, whether he forgot or failed to notice, leaves out Artemis. In anger she sends the great Calydonian boar, and the ravaging of his land and the strife that follows destroy his house.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phoenix tells this story to Achilles as a warning that neglecting what is due, even through simple forgetfulness, brings ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Oeneus is the Kural's man who ‘failed to perform the praised things’ and found no good afterwards.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Homer himself raises forgetting as a possible cause of the neglected duty; a strong match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But most people do not do these, but take refuge in theory and think they are being philosophers and will become good in this way, behaving somewhat like patients who listen attentively to their doctors, but do none of the things they are ordered to do.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle insists that virtue comes only from actually performing virtuous acts, and that those who merely admire the prescriptions are like patients who ignore their doctors.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's demand that praised deeds be done, not merely known.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 2.4 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match on the failure to do what is known to be good.

kurals.tamil:
இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக தாந்தம்
மகிழ்ச்சியின் மைந்துறும் போழ்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Ikazhchchiyin kettaarai ulluka thaandham
Makizhchchiyin maindhurum pozhdhu.
kurals.meaning: Whenever you feel strong and swollen with your own delight, remember those who were ruined through heedlessness.
kurals.elementary: When you win a prize and feel like the best in the world, it's a good moment to remember the story of the hare who was so sure of winning that he took a nap and lost to the tortoise. Remembering other people's mistakes keeps you careful.
kurals.university: இகழ்ச்சி here means heedless disregard (it shares a root with இகழ்ந்தார் in 538), and மைந்துறும் போழ்து means ‘the moment one grows strong or elated’. Parimelazhagar makes kings the subject: when they grow confident in their own pleasures, they should remember those of old who perished through the lapse such pleasure breeds. He explains that the text says ‘their own delight’ because the king owns the means of pleasure, and that it ties elation to ruin because neglect and downfall arise together. The point, he says, is that one who recalls the ruined will think ‘I too shall perish that way’ and will not grow elated. He also records a variant reading, எண்ணுக for உள்ளுக, which Pavanar attributes to Manakkudavar. Manakkudavar gives the couplet a concrete application: kings should have their food, clothing and unguents examined, that is, guard against poisoning.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The mortal king Nahusha is raised to the throne of Indra while Indra is in hiding. Intoxicated by his new power, he forces the great sages to carry his palanquin and, in his impatience, kicks Agastya. He is cursed on the spot to fall from heaven as a serpent.
hinduism.explanation: The Mahabharata tells the story as a warning of how quickly exaltation turns into ruin when power makes one careless of what is due.
hinduism.tie_back: Nahusha is exactly the kind of figure the Kural tells rulers to remember when their own delight makes them feel invincible.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Sections 11-17 (the story of Nahusha), trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: A classic Indian example of elation leading to heedless ruin, the kind of story the Kural asks rulers to recall.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come. Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.”
christianity.explanation: Paul retells Israel's failures in the wilderness and says they were recorded precisely so that the confident would remember them and take heed.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's method: when you feel secure, remember those who fell.
christianity._accuracy_note: Nearly identical logic: remembering the fallen as a check on self-confidence.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not like the exultant.” … “And We caused the earth to swallow him and his home.”
islam.explanation: Qarun's people warn him against exulting in his vast treasures. He dismisses them, and the earth swallows him, so that those who had envied him the day before learn from his end.
islam.tie_back: Qarun is held up in the Qur'an as exactly the remembered ruin the Kural prescribes for moments of elation.
islam._accuracy_note: A strong match of exultation leading to ruin, and the story is presented as a lesson for others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up so that he did corruptly, and he trespassed against the LORD his God; for he went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense.”
judaism.explanation: King Uzziah prospered greatly, but at the height of his strength he grew arrogant and overstepped, and he was struck with leprosy for the rest of his life.
judaism.tie_back: The Chronicler's ‘when he was strong’ is the Kural's மைந்துறும் போழ்து, the very moment it warns about.
judaism._accuracy_note: A close match on the moment of strength becoming the moment of fall.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Possessions, honor, and popularity came to Devadatta for his own ruin and downfall.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha points to Devadatta as the cautionary example: success and fame swelled him and led to his downfall, like a banana plant killed by its own fruit.
buddhism.tie_back: Devadatta is the kind of ruined figure the Kural tells us to call to mind when success elates us.
buddhism._accuracy_note: A strong parallel of success leading to ruin, used explicitly as a warning example.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus fits wings to his son Icarus and warns him to fly a middle course. But the boy delights in his daring flight, abandons his guide and soars higher, until the sun softens the wax and he falls into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: Icarus's fall became the classic Western example of elation making someone forget the limits he had been warned about.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He is the ruined figure the Kural bids us remember when delight makes us feel we can fly.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: An excellent illustration of exhilaration leading to forgetting a warning; not itself a teaching about remembering.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lady Philosophy reminds the imprisoned Boethius that Fortune's nature is to turn her wheel. She recalls kings brought low, such as Croesus, who was placed on the pyre and saved only by a sudden rain, and tells him that no one should trust prosperity as if it were his own.
philosophy.explanation: For Boethius, remembering the fallen is the cure for the illusion that good fortune is permanent.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's remedy of recalling the ruined when one is swollen with success.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased. The same use of fallen examples to check confidence in prosperity.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளியது எய்தல் எளிதுமன் மற்றுந்தான்
உள்ளியது உள்ளப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ulliyadhu eydhal elidhuman matrundhaan
Ulliyadhu ullap perin.
kurals.meaning: Reaching what you have set your mind on is easy, as long as you can keep thinking of it steadily from then on.
kurals.elementary: If you want to learn to ride a bike, you have to keep that goal in your mind every day, even after you fall. Kids who keep thinking about their goal and don't let it slip away usually get there.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on repeating உள்ளியது (‘what was thought of’) together with the verb உள்ளு (‘to think of, keep in mind’): attaining your aim is easy if you can ‘think again what you thought’. Parimelazhagar reads it as advice to a king: he will easily obtain what he intended, exactly as he intended it, if he can keep thinking of that same thing, which he explains as striving towards it without forgetting. He takes மன் as an ஒழியிசை particle, one that implies an unspoken ‘but that is hard to manage’, so the couplet quietly admits that sustained attention is the difficult part. Pavanar rejects this analysis of மன் as unsuitable here and takes மற்று to mean ‘afterwards, further’. Manakkudavar reads the couplet as the requirement to remember, above all, what one first resolved. Parimelazhagar groups 539-540 as the means (உபாயம்) for achieving unforgetfulness.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Drona tests his pupils by setting a wooden bird on a treetop and asking each what he sees. The others describe the tree, the branches, their brothers and their teacher, and are sent away. Arjuna says he sees only the bird's head, is told to shoot, and brings it down.
hinduism.explanation: The episode is the classic Indian image of a mind that holds unwaveringly to what it has aimed at.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna embodies the Kural's formula: to keep thinking of what one has set one's mind on is to attain it easily.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Sambhava Parva), Drona's test of the Kuru princes, trans. K. M. Ganguli
hinduism._accuracy_note: A vivid narrative match for single-minded, unforgetting focus on one's aim.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes a life gathered into ‘this one thing’: fixing on the goal ahead and pressing towards it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it presents steady, single-minded attention to the goal as the way to reach it.
christianity._accuracy_note: A close match on unwavering focus on the aim; Paul's goal is spiritual rather than worldly.

islam.quote_or_event: “The reward of deeds depends upon the intentions and every person will get the reward according to what he has intended.”
islam.explanation: The opening hadith of Bukhari makes the intention held in the heart the determining factor in what a person obtains from his deeds.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too ties attainment to what one keeps firmly in mind.
islam._accuracy_note: Links attainment to what is intended, but the hadith is about the moral worth of deeds, not about achieving goals through sustained attention.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I have set the LORD always before me; Surely He is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist describes keeping his focus constantly before his eyes, and finds in that steadiness the source of his firmness.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links continual remembrance of one's aim with unshakeable success.
judaism._accuracy_note: The same pattern of constant focus leading to steadfastness; the object here is God rather than a chosen goal.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All compounded things are subject to vanish. Strive with earnestness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha repeats this exhortation near the end of his life, and it is echoed in his final words (appamādena sampādetha, ‘accomplish the goal through heedfulness’). He makes unremitting heedfulness the one thing to hold to until the goal is reached.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's key to attainment is keeping one's aim before the mind without lapse, which is the Buddha's own last counsel.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta) §3.63, trans. Sister Vajira and Francis Story
buddhism._accuracy_note: The quoted words are the §3.63 exhortation; the final-words connection is noted in prose. Strong match on heedfulness as the means to the goal.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Atalanta, the swiftest runner, can beat any suitor. Hippomenes drops three golden apples from Aphrodite during their race, and each time Atalanta turns aside to pick one up. She loses the race she would certainly have won.
greek_mythology.explanation: Atalanta loses not through weakness but because her attention is pulled away from the finish line.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She is the opposite of the Kural's ideal: had she kept her mind on what she aimed at, winning would have been easy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A clear negative illustration of losing a sure goal through distraction.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “My experience is what I agree to attend to.”
philosophy.explanation: William James argues that selective, sustained attention shapes what a person's mind and life actually become.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural likewise makes steady attention to one's aim the decisive condition for achieving it.
philosophy.source: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), ch. 11 ‘Attention’
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the primacy of sustained attention; James is describing how experience is formed, not a recipe for success.
